source.trailTitle: How far the paper trail actually runs
trail: Wikiquote carries the line in its sourced quotes section, under the heading Reality…What a Concept (1979) — Robin Williams, Wikiquote ↗. Its neighbours in that list are a Mister Rogers parody and a Shakespeare send-up, both very much Williams’s territory.
Read the page’s underlying wikitext ↗ and the problem shows: not one bullet in that album section has a footnote, track number or timestamp. The album title is the citation.

Downstream quote sites reproduce the wording identically and cite the same 1979 album — and QuotePark ↗ says plainly that its entry was adopted from Wikiquote. That is one source wearing several hats, not independent corroboration.
Quote Investigator ↗, the usual court of last resort for lines like this, has no article on it — so there is no specialist finding to defer to, in either direction.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller context to give. The line is reproduced here exactly as Wikiquote carries it; no transcript of the surrounding routine, and no audio of the credited album, could be located to show what came before or after it.
source.rightsHolder: The Estate of Robin Williams; the credited album was issued by Casablanca Records
source.rightsNote: Whatever performance this line came from, it is a 20th-century stand-up routine by a performer who died in 2014 — nowhere near the public domain, which in the United States currently reaches only works first published before 1931. The credited album, Reality…What a Concept, was recorded at a 1979 live show and issued by Casablanca Records that year; rights sit with Williams’s estate and the label. Treat the text as protected.

author.name: Robin Williams
author.heading: About Robin Williams
author.bio: Born in Chicago on 21 July 1951, Robin Williams began performing stand-up in the San Francisco Bay Area in 1976, working his way up from tending bar at the Holy City Zoo before moving to Los Angeles and the Comedy Store. National fame arrived with the alien Mork in ABC’s Mork & Mindy (1978–1982), a part he improvised heavily — and in the same stretch he won a Grammy for Best Comedy Album for the recording of his 1979 live show at the Copacabana in New York, Reality…What a Concept. He died on 11 August 2014 in Paradise Cay, California.

misattribution.heading: Not a wrong name — a citation that eats its own tail
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is claiming this joke. The trouble is subtler and more common: a confident-looking source citation that, followed backwards, arrives at a single unsourced line and stops.

items.why: Every quote page that offers a source offers that album — and QuotePark ↗ states outright that its entry was adopted from Wikiquote. The wording is byte-identical across sites, which is what copying looks like, not what independent attestation looks like.

The raw wikitext ↗ shows the album heading carries the whole section: no track, no timestamp, no reference tag on this line or any other line under it. A work heading is a claim about a source, not a source.

A search of QI for “chairs” ↗ turns up nothing on this joke. That is not evidence against Williams — it simply means no one has done the archival work, so there is no earliest-attestation date to hand anyone.

Williams is one of the internet’s great quote magnets, and an improviser by trade — Wikipedia ↗ notes he improvised much of his material, including his Mork & Mindy dialogue. That cuts both ways: it makes the line entirely in character, and it makes a fixed, quotable text harder to pin down.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest position: no evidence contradicts Robin Williams, and the line sits in Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ under his 1979 album — but until someone cites a track, a timestamp or a transcript, “attributed” is as far as the evidence reaches.

context.heading: Why this one is hard to nail down
lead: 1979 was the year the comedy world caught up with Robin Williams. He had come up through Bay Area clubs from 1976, starting at the Holy City Zoo, and by then was starring as Mork on Mork & Mindy, a role he largely improvised ↗. That same year he taped a live show at the Copacabana in New York; the resulting album, Reality…What a Concept, took the Grammy for Best Comedy Album among the 1980 winners ↗.

An improviser’s best throwaway lines are exactly the ones that resist citation. A novelist’s sentence sits on a numbered page forever; a comic’s aside exists in a particular room on a particular night, and may or may not have survived onto the record. That is the gap this quote lives in — utterly plausible as Williams, and stubbornly unsourced.
context.pull: A work heading is a claim about a source. It is not a source.
